new.title: Visit Horta's very first town house in Schaerbeek
new.desc: Maison Autrique, designed in 1893 for an engineer friend, is where Victor Horta first tried out Art Nouveau in a home. The commune of Schaerbeek bought and restored it, and you can wander from cellar to attic.
new.tip: It is far less crowded than the Horta Museum. Combine it with a stroll up the Chaussée de Haecht to the Sainte-Marie church.
new.q: Maison Autrique, Chaussée de Haecht 266, Schaerbeek

new.title: Find the skinniest house on Square Ambiorix
new.desc: Maison Saint-Cyr, by Gustave Strauven, squeezes a whole riot of curling wrought iron onto a facade only a few metres wide. It is one of the wildest Art Nouveau fronts in the city.
new.tip: It is a private home, so admire it from the square, then walk down through the sloping Square Marie-Louise with its pond and grotto.
new.q: Maison Saint-Cyr, Square Ambiorix 11, Brussels

new.title: Read the sgraffito facade of Maison Cauchie
new.desc: Painter Paul Cauchie turned his own 1905 house in Etterbeek into an advertisement for his craft: the whole front is covered in sgraffito figures of women and the motto 'Par Nous, Pour Nous'.
new.tip: The facade is free to see at any time; the interior only opens on a few days, so check the house's website before planning to go in.
new.q: Maison Cauchie, Rue des Francs 5, Etterbeek

new.title: Peek at the Palais Stoclet from the Avenue de Tervueren
new.desc: This UNESCO-listed mansion by Viennese architect Josef Hoffmann hides Gustav Klimt mosaics inside. Its white marble cube and stepped tower look decades ahead of the 1900s houses around it.
new.tip: The house is private and closed to visitors, so enjoy the outside, then ride tram 44 or 39 further out to Woluwe Park.
new.q: Palais Stoclet, Avenue de Tervueren 281, Woluwe-Saint-Pierre

new.title: Find Rodin's Thinker among the graves of Laeken
new.desc: Laeken Cemetery, the city's oldest still in use, is full of 19th-century funerary art, and an original bronze cast of Rodin's Thinker sits on one tomb. Next door, the Notre-Dame de Laeken church holds the royal crypt.
new.tip: Look for the small museum of the Salu sculpture workshop by the entrance; it explains how the monuments around you were made.
new.q: Cimetière de Laeken, Parvis Notre-Dame, Laeken

new.title: Climb up to the dome of Koekelberg Basilica
new.desc: The National Basilica of the Sacred Heart is one of the largest churches in the world, an Art Deco giant in green copper at the end of a long boulevard. From the gallery at the top you look right across Brussels.
new.tip: Entry to the church is free; the panorama at the top has its own ticket. Metro Simonis is a short walk away.
new.q: Basilique de Koekelberg

new.title: Visit the flat where Magritte painted in Jette
new.desc: From 1930 to 1954 René Magritte and Georgette rented the ground floor of this ordinary Jette house, and he painted around 800 works here. The rooms are rebuilt as they lived in them, with letters, photos and drawings upstairs.
new.tip: This is not the big Magritte Museum on Place Royale; it is a much more personal visit, and there is a free guided tour on the last Wednesday of the month.
new.q: Musée René Magritte, Rue Esseghem 135, Jette

new.title: Get lost in the Van Buuren labyrinth in Uccle
new.desc: A banker couple filled their 1920s Art Deco villa with art from the 15th to the 20th century. Behind it, Alice van Buuren had a hedge labyrinth built around a century-old cedar, plus a heart-shaped garden in memory of her husband.
new.tip: Book your slot online; then walk on to Wolvendael Park and the Dieweg cemetery, both close by.
new.q: Musée et Jardins Van Buuren, Avenue Léo Errera 41, Uccle

new.title: Pay your respects to Hergé at the Dieweg cemetery
new.desc: Closed to burials since 1958, this Uccle cemetery has been swallowed by ivy and trees, with more than 200 plant species among the tombs. Tintin's creator Hergé lies here, along with Art Nouveau architect Paul Hankar and a tomb designed by Victor Horta.
new.tip: Autumn is when it is at its most atmospheric. Tram 92 stops at Dieweg; keep an eye out for the resident foxes.
new.q: Cimetière du Dieweg, Dieweg 95, Uccle

new.title: Stroll the garden cities of Le Logis and Floréal
new.desc: Built from 1921 in Watermael-Boitsfort, these cottage estates have brightly painted shutters, winding footpaths, hedges and streets named after flowers and birds. In spring, rows of Japanese cherry trees turn the lanes pink.
new.tip: Start at the visitor centre on Place Joseph Wauters, which runs guided walks; come in April for the blossom.
new.q: Place Joseph Wauters, Watermael-Boitsfort

new.title: Walk the monks' ponds at Rouge-Cloître
new.desc: This 14th-century priory on the edge of the Sonian Forest in Auderghem sits among the fish ponds its monks dug, now a nature reserve full of waterfowl. The old buildings house an art centre and a storytelling theatre.
new.tip: Finish at the Relais Forestier tavern by the gate; bring cash, as it does not take cards. Tram 8 stops nearby at Rouge-Cloître.
new.q: Rouge-Cloître, Rue du Rouge-Cloître 4, Auderghem

new.title: See contemporary art in the old Wielemans brewery
new.desc: Wiels occupies a 1931 modernist brewhouse in Forest that was once the largest in continental Europe. The copper brewing kettles still stand in the café, and the galleries upstairs show changing contemporary art.
new.tip: Go up to the rooftop for a view over the south of the city, then walk across to Forest Park.
new.q: WIELS, Avenue Van Volxem 354, Forest

new.title: Find Erasmus in the old village heart of Anderlecht
new.desc: The humanist Erasmus stayed in this Gothic house in 1521, and it now holds his books, paintings and a philosophical garden. Around it, cobbled Rue Porselein and the Place de la Vaillance feel like a village that Brussels forgot to swallow.
new.tip: Look into the tiny beguinage museum nearby, and save room for lunch at Friture René on the Place de la Résistance.
new.q: Maison d'Erasme, Rue de Formanoir 31, Anderlecht

new.title: Watch the sails turn at Anderlecht's Luizenmolen
new.desc: On the rural western edge of Anderlecht stands a rebuilt 19th-century windmill, a reminder that this was farmland not long ago. It is one of the few working windmills inside the Brussels region.
new.tip: The mill opens to visitors on the second and fourth Sunday of the month; on other days enjoy it from the fields of the Pajottenland edge.
new.q: Luizenmolen, Rue des Papillons 192, Anderlecht

new.title: Slip into the hidden lane of Rue de la Cigogne
new.desc: Behind an archway off Rue de Flandre runs a quiet, curving lane of little cottages hung with wisteria, one of the old 'impasses' where working families once lived. A few doors away, a covered passage leads to La Bellone, a baroque facade under a glass roof.
new.tip: Come between April and June for the wisteria, and enter from Rue du Rempart des Moines if the Rue de Flandre side is closed.
new.q: Rue de la Cigogne, Bruxelles

new.title: Look over the rooftops from the Royal Library
new.desc: KBR, the 1930s national library at the Mont des Arts, has a museum of medieval manuscripts and an upper floor with a panoramic view over the lower town to the town hall spire.
new.tip: Afterwards, walk down the Mont des Arts gardens at sunset, when the view across to the Grand-Place glows.
new.q: KBR Royal Library of Belgium, Mont des Arts, Brussels

new.title: Discover the follies of Parc Pierre Paulus in Saint-Gilles
new.desc: This small English-style park in Saint-Gilles hides fake ruins and cascades, next to Maison Pelgrims, a 1905 mansion with an Art Deco interior and a winter garden.
new.tip: The mansion opens when it hosts exhibitions; the park is always worth a detour on the way to the Parvis de Saint-Gilles.
new.q: Maison Pelgrims, Rue de Parme 69, Saint-Gilles

new.title: Admire the Byzantine domes of Sainte-Marie in Schaerbeek
new.desc: At the top of Rue Royale, the Église Royale Sainte-Marie mixes Byzantine domes with Gothic touches and has stained glass by Capronnier. It is one of the most unexpected silhouettes in Brussels.
new.tip: Tram 92 passes right by it; carry on north to the Halles de Schaerbeek and the Chaussée de Haecht.
new.q: Église Royale Sainte-Marie, Place de la Reine, Schaerbeek

new.title: Taste the prize-winning frites at Master Frites
new.desc: This Schaerbeek friterie, run by brothers who came to Brussels from Kosovo, was voted the best fry shop in the city. Fries are cut on site and fried twice, served in a paper cone, and you can actually sit down to eat them.
new.tip: It is near Place Meiser on the Chaussée de Louvain; there is a smaller takeaway counter in Ixelles too.
new.q: Master Frites, Chaussée de Louvain 503, Schaerbeek

new.title: Order moules-frites at Friture René in Anderlecht
new.desc: A family restaurant since 1932, with checked tablecloths and the classics of Brussels home cooking: mussels, steak, frites and stoemp, served without fuss.
new.tip: It is a few minutes from Maison d'Erasme and the Saint-Guidon metro stop; book ahead on weekends.
new.q: Friture René, Place de la Résistance 14, Anderlecht

new.title: Explore rare beers at Moeder Lambic in Saint-Gilles
new.desc: An old-fashioned brown café near the Saint-Gilles town hall, with several hundred unusual beers, many from small Belgian brewers, and a serious lambic list.
new.tip: Ask the staff for something local on draught rather than reading the whole menu.
new.q: Moeder Lambic, Rue de Savoie 68, Saint-Gilles

new.title: Have a drink on the Parvis at Le Verschueren
new.desc: This neighbourhood institution on the Parvis de Saint-Gilles still shows the wooden league table of long-vanished football clubs on its wall. The square outside is the social heart of Saint-Gilles.
new.tip: Grab a terrace seat on a sunny afternoon, or come on a market morning when the Parvis fills with stalls.
new.q: Brasserie Verschueren, Parvis de Saint-Gilles 11, Saint-Gilles

new.title: Drink a Zinnebir at the Brasserie de la Senne
new.desc: The Senne brewery, named after the river buried under Brussels, makes hoppy and barrel-aged beers that locals drink everywhere. Its Zennebar sits right at the brewery next to Tour & Taxis.
new.tip: Ask what is fresh from the tanks; the brewery shop next door sells bottles to take home.
new.q: Brasserie de la Senne, Drève Anna Boch 19, Brussels

new.title: Taste a new brew at the Brussels Beer Project
new.desc: This young brewery on Rue Antoine Dansaert brews experimental beers on site and pours them in its taproom, a modern counterweight to the city's centuries-old lambic tradition.
new.tip: Try a flight of small glasses to compare; it is a short walk from Sainte-Catherine.
new.q: Brussels Beer Project, Rue Antoine Dansaert 188, Brussels

new.title: Eat mussels by the kilo at Le Pré Salé
new.desc: A former butcher's shop on Rue de Flandre where mussels come in big pots by the kilo alongside other Brussels classics.
new.tip: Mussels are best in season from late summer to winter; book, as locals fill it quickly.
new.q: Le Pré Salé, Rue de Flandre 20, Brussels

new.title: Play chess over a beer at Le Greenwich
new.desc: A wood-panelled brown café from another age where regulars sit over chessboards and talk in low voices.
new.tip: Bring a friend and ask for a board; keep your voice down, it is part of the charm.
new.q: Le Greenwich, Rue des Chartreux 7, Brussels

new.title: Take the ferry to Chalet Robinson
new.desc: In the middle of the lake in the Bois de la Cambre sits a wooden chalet on its own little island, reached by a short ferry crossing. It is the most Brussels way to have a drink in the park.
new.tip: Walk the lake loop first; on Sundays the park roads are closed to cars and fill with cyclists and skaters.
new.q: Chalet Robinson, Bois de la Cambre, Brussels

new.title: Eat a cone of Frit Flagey by the Ixelles ponds
new.desc: The friterie on Place Flagey is a neighbourhood favourite, with crisp fries and a queue of students and locals at all hours, right next to the ocean liner shaped Flagey building.
new.tip: Take your cone across the road and eat it on a bench by the Ixelles ponds.
new.q: Frit Flagey, Place Eugène Flagey, Ixelles

new.title: Toast among 2,000 bottles at the Schaerbeek Beer Museum
new.desc: This little museum is filled with over 2,000 Belgian beer bottles, old brewing gear and a little tavern, and a tasting is part of the visit.
new.tip: It only opens a couple of afternoons a week, so check the days before heading out.
new.q: Musée de la Bière de Schaerbeek, Avenue Louis Bertrand 33, Schaerbeek

new.title: Graze the Friday evening market at Chasseurs Ardennais
new.desc: Every Friday evening this little Schaerbeek square turns into a neighbourhood party, with food stalls, food trucks and mobile wine bars instead of vegetables.
new.tip: Come straight after work and bring a friend; it is a short walk from Square Ambiorix.
new.q: Place des Chasseurs Ardennais, Schaerbeek

new.title: Brave a mitraillette at Fritland
new.desc: The mitraillette, a baguette stuffed with meat, frites and sauce, is Brussels' ultimate late-night snack, and this busy friterie near the Bourse is the classic place to try one.
new.tip: Pay cash at the counter and share one; it is bigger than it looks.
new.q: Fritland, Rue Henri Maus 49, Brussels

new.title: Hunt for a rare Trappist at Bier Circus
new.desc: A no-nonsense beer bar near the Cirque Royal with a long list of rare beers, Trappists and lambics, far from the tourist taps around the Grand-Place.
new.tip: Ask for a gueuze or kriek from a small producer you have not heard of.
new.q: Bier Circus, Rue de l'Enseignement 57, Brussels

new.title: Follow the Meyboom tree to its planting
new.desc: Every 9 August, a tradition dating back to at least 1308, a beech is carried from the Bois de la Cambre through the streets with brass bands and giants, and planted at the corner of Rue des Sables and Rue du Marais. It is recognised by UNESCO.
new.tip: Catch the procession on the Grand-Place in the early afternoon, then follow it to the planting; people take home a small branch for luck.
new.q: Rue des Sables et Rue du Marais, Bruxelles

new.title: Watch the Ommegang parade leave the Sablon
new.desc: Around the turn of June and July, some 1,400 people in Renaissance costume, with horses, crossbowmen and giants, re-enact the 1549 entry of Charles V into Brussels. The pageant is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
new.tip: The procession through the streets is free to watch from the Sablon; the final show on the Grand-Place needs a seat ticket.
new.q: Église Notre-Dame du Sablon, Bruxelles

new.title: Skate and stroll through Plaisirs d'Hiver
new.desc: From late November to early January, chalets fill the old fish market around Sainte-Catherine, a Ferris wheel turns, an ice rink opens on Place De Brouckère and a sound and light show plays on the Grand-Place.
new.tip: Go on a weeknight to avoid the crowds, and pair a mulled wine with a plate of escargots from a stall.
new.q: Place Sainte-Catherine, Bruxelles

new.title: See a puppet show in Brusselian at Toone
new.desc: Since about 1830 the Toone family has run Brussels' last traditional rod-marionette theatre, now hidden down an alley off Rue du Marché aux Herbes. Plays are performed in the old Brussels dialect, full of 'zwanze' humour.
new.tip: Even without a show, have a beer in the theatre's estaminet and look round the little puppet museum next door.
new.q: Théâtre Royal de Toone, Rue du Marché aux Herbes 66, Bruxelles

new.title: Go underground at the Sewer Museum
new.desc: At the Porte d'Anderlecht you descend into the city's 1,900 km sewer network and see the hidden River Senne, vaulted over in the 19th century, still flowing below the streets.
new.tip: Join a guided tour to hear the stories; wear shoes you do not mind getting a little damp.
new.q: Musée des Égouts, Porte d'Anderlecht, Bruxelles

new.title: Spend a lazy afternoon in Parc Josaphat
new.desc: Schaerbeek's big landscaped park in a valley has ponds, a rose garden, sculptures and an open-air theatre, and almost no tourists.
new.tip: Look for the hilltop knoll behind the tennis courts for a view over the park; tram 7 runs along its edge.
new.q: Parc Josaphat, Schaerbeek

new.title: Ride a vintage tram from the Woluwe depot
new.desc: The Brussels Tram Museum keeps around 130 vehicles, from horse-drawn trams to old buses, in a historic depot on the Avenue de Tervueren. Many still run, and on summer weekends you can ride one.
new.tip: Woluwe Park is right across the road; check the museum's calendar for heritage tram runs.
new.q: Musée du Tram, Avenue de Tervueren 364b, Woluwe-Saint-Pierre

new.title: Climb aboard old locomotives at Train World
new.desc: In and around the restored Schaerbeek station, Belgium's railway museum shows steam engines and royal carriages in sets designed by comic artist François Schuiten.
new.tip: Arrive by train: Schaerbeek station is part of the museum itself.
new.q: Train World, Place Princesse Élisabeth 5, Schaerbeek

new.title: Cheer for Union Saint-Gilloise at the Joseph Marien stadium
new.desc: Union SG, the club of Saint-Gilles and Forest, plays in a small old stadium set in Parc Duden. It is one of the most atmospheric football grounds in Belgium.
new.tip: Tickets for big games sell out; arrive early and climb the park slope to soak up the pre-match mood.
new.q: Stade Joseph Marien, Chaussée de Bruxelles 223, Forest

new.title: Walk across Europe in an afternoon at Mini-Europe
new.desc: At the foot of the Atomium, Europe's landmarks stand at 1:25 scale, from Big Ben to the Acropolis, with working models and moving trains.
new.tip: Combine it with the Atomium on the same day; it is most fun on a sunny afternoon.
new.q: Mini-Europe, Bruparck, Bruxelles

new.title: Walk to the Pelouse des Anglais in the Sonian Forest
new.desc: Deep in the forest beyond the Bois de la Cambre lies a clearing where, the story goes, English soldiers played cricket on the eve of Waterloo in 1815. Around it, the tall beeches of the Sonian Forest begin.
new.tip: Walk in from the Bois de la Cambre or the old Boitsfort hippodrome; stay on marked paths.
new.q: Pelouse des Anglais, Forêt de Soignes, Bruxelles

new.title: Shop the weekend market under the Abattoir's iron roof
new.desc: Under a listed 1890 cast-iron hall in Cureghem, guarded by two cast-iron bulls, around 100,000 people a week come for the Friday to Sunday market: meat, fish, spices, vegetables and everything else.
new.tip: Go early in the morning; Clemenceau metro station is opposite.
new.q: Abattoir, Rue Ropsy-Chaudron 24, Anderlecht

new.title: Look down on Brussels from Laeken Park
new.desc: Leopold II's park slopes up to the neo-Gothic Dynasty Monument, from where the city spreads out below. Down the hill stands a copy of Bologna's Neptune fountain.
new.tip: Combine it with the Royal Greenhouses in spring, or the Atomium a short walk to the west.
new.q: Monument à la Dynastie, Parc de Laeken
